Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-145, and 147-152 are pending for examination with claim
1 being independent.

Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-141, 143-144, 147-149, and 151-152 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Publication No. 2010/0297686 to Gogotsi et al. ("Gogotsi") in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2013/0338627 to Rylander et al. ("Rylander").

The Patent Office alleges that Gogotsi teaches each and every feature of independent claim 1, except for: (i) an end portion having a substantially constant average cross-sectional diameter of less than 100 nm; (ii) the end portion having a length of between about 750 micrometers and about

3 mm; and (iii) a tapered portion having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers. Regarding (i), the Patent Office alleges that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the diameter of the end portion of Gogotsi from about 100-150 nm to be less than 100 nm (see page 5 of the Office Action). The Patent Office further alleges that (ii) and (iii) are taught by Rylander, and that it would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art to combine Gogotsi and Rylander with a reasonable expectation of success (see page 6 of the Office Action). It is believed, however, that this rejection is deficient and should be withdrawn for at least the following reasons.

body.p: The Patent Office alleges that Gogotsi discloses a member comprising a tapered portion connecting the starting portion to the end portion (see page 4 of the Office Action), but concedes

that Gogotsi fails to teach that the tapered portion has a length of no more than about 500 micrometers (see page 6 of the Office Action). The Patent Office further alleges that Rylander discloses a tapered portion having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers and that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the length of the tapered portion of Gogotsi with the length of the tapered portion of Rylander (see page 6 of the Office Action).

In particular, the Patent Office alleges that one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to decrease the length of the tapered portion of the member in Gogotsi because doing so would have provided a larger surface area for attaching particles, thereby increasing the SERS signal during characterization (see page 6 of the Office Action). Gogotsi, however, describes probes including an acicular member having a distal end surmounted by a population of metallic nanoparticles. Since the particles are surmounted only on the distal end of the probe in Gogotsi, it is not seen how decreasing the length of any tapered portion of the probe in Gogotsi would have provided a larger surface area for attaching particles, as alleged by the Patent Office. Indeed, increasing the length of the distal end of the probe in Gogotsi would have provided a larger surface area for attaching particles, but decreasing the length of any tapered portion of the probe in Gogotsi would have had no effect on the population of particles attached to the distal end, i.e., the same number of particles could be attached to the distal end of the probe in Gogotsi regardless of the size of the tapered portion. Therefore, Gogotsi provides no teaching, suggestion, or motivation to decrease the length of any tapered portion of the probe described therein, and the Patent Office has not met its burden in providing a rationale to support a conclusion that independent claim 1 would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art (see M.P.E.P. § 2143(I)(G)).
IL One of ordinary skill in the art would have had no reasonable expectation of success in modifving the length of the tapered portion of Gogotsi with the length of the tapered portion
The Patent Office alleges that one of ordinary skill in the art would have had a reasonable
expectation of success in modifying the length of the tapered portion of the member in Gogotsi with the length of the tapered portion in Rylander (see page 6 of the Office Action).
In response to the Office Action dated September 8, 2023, Applicant argued that one of

ordinary skill in the art seeking to modify the length of any tapered portion of the probe in Gogotsi with the length of the tapered portion of the device in Rylander would not have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so, at least because the technique of pulling glass capillaries taught in Gogotsi is incapable of producing tapered portions of such short dimensions, as evidenced by instructions from Sutter Instrument, titled "Creating a Pipette with a Short Taper and a 25p to 35p Tip" ("Sutter"). In particular, paragraph [0070] of Gogotsi describes that the acicular glass probes described therein are prepared by pulling a borosilicate glass capillary using a laser-based micropipette puller from Sutter Instrument, and Sutter describes that such glass pulling techniques result in tapers that are on the millimeter scale (3 mm to 4 mm, i.e., at least 6-8 times longer, at best, than the 500 micrometer maximum length of the tapered portion as recited in independent claim 1).

The Patent Office now alleges that: (i) there are a number of variables that can influence the shape of pulled glass; and (ii) one of ordinary skill in the art would understand that achieving a desired shape or length of the glass is a matter of optimizing a set of operating parameters and conditions (see page 13 of the Office Action).

Submitted herewith is a Declaration of Qimin Quan under 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 ("the Declaration") establishing that the technique of pulling glass capillaries taught in Gogotsi is incapable of producing tapered portions having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers, as recited in independent claim 1. The Declaration further establishes that none of the variables listed on page 13 of the Office Action can be optimized to produce a probe with a tapered portion having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers. For example, the Declaration refers to: (i) a catalog from Sutter Instruments, titled "Sutter Instrument 50 Years," which is available via the web at https://www.sutter.com/PDFs/SutterCatalog.pdf ("Sutter Catalog"); and (ii) an infographic from World Precision Instruments, titled "How to Choose a Puller," which is available via the web at https://www.wpiinc.com/pub/media/wysiwyg/pdf/infographics/Puller-ComparisonIG.pdf ("WPI Infographic"). Both Sutter Catalog and WPI Infographic compare various types of pullers having different types of filaments, including the P-2000 puller used in Gogotsi (see page 178 of Sutter Catalog), but these pullers only produce taper lengths on the millimeter or centimeter scale. As should be appreciated by the Patent Office, neither of these documents from major manufacturers in
the glass capillary and glassing pulling field discuss taper lengths of no more than about 500 micrometers, as recited in independent claim 1.
The Declaration is consistent with: (i) page 7, lines 3-9 of the application as filed, which

states that tapered portions having a length of 500 micrometers or less are difficult to achieve using glass pulling techniques, which instead result in long (often meters) tapered portions; (ii) Sutter, Sutter Catalog, and WPI infographic, all of which are evidence that borosilicate glass capillaries cannot be pulled to produce tapered portions of such short dimensions; (iii) Gogotsi, which nowhere teaches or suggests that such dimensions could have been produced, e.g., using the Sutter Instrument; and (iv) page 8, lines 4-18 of the application as filed in conjunction with Figs. 1F-1G, which states that members (and their tapered portions) having such dimensions may be formed using various etching techniques. Therefore, in view of the Declaration, and the other cited evidence, there would have been no reasonable expectation of success for one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the length of any tapered portion of the probe in Gogotsi with the length of the tapered portion in Rylander. The Patent Office has not met its burden in providing a rationale to support a conclusion that independent claim 1 would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art (see M.P.E.P. § 2143(I)(G)), especially given that the skilled person, following the teachings of Gogotsi and using the Sutter Instrument, could not reasonably have achieved such short dimensions.

The Patent Office is reminded that the key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious, and the mere identification in the prior art of each component (which is not conceded in this case) does not show that the combination as a whole lacks the necessary attributes for patentability (see M.P.E.P. § 2142). In the Office Action, the Patent Office appears to be picking and choosing various dimensions of various portions of devices from different references that are formed by different techniques without providing a rationale for the motivation or reasonable expectation of success in doing so, and while disregarding the express teachings of the cited references. Accordingly, the rejection of independent claim 1 is based on impermissible hindsight (see M.P.E.P. § 2145(X)(A)), using the teachings of the instant specification as a road map, and not the disclosure of the cited references as they would have been considered by a person of ordinary skill in the art.

Indeed, while the prior art is presumed to be enabling (see M.P.E.P. § 2121), the presumption of operability of a prior art reference may be rebutted by a declaration (see M.P.E.P. § 716.07), as is this case here regarding the Patent Office's proposed (but inoperable) combination of Gogotsi and Rylander to allege that a tapered portion having a length of no more than about 500 micrometers would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art.
III. Gogotsi fails to teach or render non-inventive a member formed by etching, as recited in

Furthermore, without conceding to the merits of the rejection, independent claim 1 has been amended to recite that the member is formed by etching. Gogotsi does not teach or make obvious, at least, this feature. Instead, as explained above in Section II, Gogotsi describes that the acicular glass probes described therein are prepared by glass pulling techniques (see, for example, paragraph [0070] of Gogotsi). In fact, Gogotsi teaches away from probes formed by etching techniques (see M.P.E.P. § 2145(X)(D)). In particular, paragraph [0022] of Gogotsi explains that a TERS silver probe shown in FIG. 16(c) was prepared by electrochemical etching, and paragraph [0099] of Gogotsi then states that such a probe has a large apex angle which is an obstacle in using it for cell probing. Accordingly, in view of the explicit teaching away of Gogotsi, there would have been no motivation or reasonable expectation of success for one of ordinary skill in the art to substitute the glass pulling techniques described in Gogotsi with the etching techniques described in Rylander.
IV. Conclusion
For at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Gogotsi and Rylander does

render amended independent claim 1 obvious, and claim 1 is patentable over the combination of Gogotsi and Rylander. The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from independent claim 1, and are therefore also patentable over the combination of Gogotsi and Rylander for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, it is not conceded that Gogotsi or Rylander, alone or in combination, teach or render obvious any of the features recited in claims 1-3,
5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-141, 143-144, 147-149, and 151-152, as asserted by the Patent Office. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.
